summary: This unit teaches you to make bread rolls, loaves and other yeast goods: how yeast works, how to weigh, mix, knead, prove, shape and bake a dough, and how to correct faults. It includes Jamaican hard dough bread, coco bread and fried doughnuts, and how to cool, store, label and present yeast goods and plan the baking so they are fresh for service.

blocks.p: This unit covers the baking of yeast goods in a hotel, villa or bakery kitchen, from weighing the flour to presenting warm rolls. It is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees. Yeast dough is alive. It needs warmth, food, moisture and time, and the baker's job is to give it the right conditions at each stage and to stop at the right moment.

Bread is on every Jamaican table: hard dough bread for the morning, coco bread with a patty, buns at Easter and rolls on a hotel dinner menu. A baker who plans the work well sends out fresh, even, golden products on time.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks in the Centre's kitchen. In practical work you make a straight dough and shape rolls, then hard dough bread loaves and coco bread. The assessor watches your hygiene, weighing, kneading, proving, shaping, baking and clean-up as well as the finished products.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work, photograph the food, your hands and the work area. Do not photograph a person's face unless they agree and the Centre allows it.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Every food handler in Jamaica must hold a **Food Handler's Permit** from the local health department. Renew it as the department says.
Wear a clean uniform and apron and cover all your hair. Keep nails short and clean. Take off rings, bracelets and watches.
**Wash your hands** with soap and warm water before you start, after touching your face or hair, after the bin or the toilet, and after a break.
Cover a cut with a **blue waterproof plaster** and a glove, so that a lost plaster can be seen in the dough.
If you are ill with vomiting, diarrhoea or fever, tell your supervisor and stay off food work.
Do not eat raw dough: raw flour and raw egg can carry germs, and yeast dough can make you unwell if you eat it raw.

head: Allergen
Where it is found in yeast goods
rows: Almost every bread made with wheat flour
Butter, milk, enriched doughs, glazes, cream fillings
Egg wash, brioche, enriched doughs, custard fillings
Seeds on rolls and loaves (a common allergen)

blocks.p: List the allergens on the label of every product. Check the recipe and the ingredient labels if a guest asks. Do not guess.

head: Hazard
How you prevent harm
rows: To check the dough, **switch off and wait for the hook to stop**
Never put a hand or a scraper in a moving bowl
Keep guards on and hands clear; switch off and unplug before cleaning.
Use a peel to put loaves in a deck oven
Deep fryer or pan of oil (doughnuts)
Use a bread knife with a sawing action on a non-slip board; keep fingers clear.
Wipe up at once so nobody slips; flour dust can irritate the chest.
Lifting heavy flour bags and dough
Bend your knees, keep your back straight, or ask for help.

blocks.note: Cool a burn under cool running water for at least 10 minutes. Report all burns and cuts and record them in the accident book.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Scrape off dough
Wash with hot water and detergent
Rinse
Sanitise
Dry

blocks.p: Dried dough is hard to remove, so soak the bowl, hook and tools in cold water at once. Use **cold** water on dough, because hot water makes it gluey. Switch off and unplug the mixer before cleaning it.

**Yeast** is a tiny living organism, a kind of fungus. It feeds on sugar and gives off **carbon dioxide gas** and a little alcohol. This is **fermentation**. The gas is trapped by the gluten and makes the dough rise. The alcohol adds flavour, and it burns off in the oven.
Yeast needs four things to work: **food** (sugar from the flour or added sugar), **warmth**, **moisture** and **time**.

head: Condition
Effect on yeast
rows: Slows it right down: dough can be kept overnight and baked next morning.
Ideal for mixing. It should feel only warm on the wrist.
Kills the yeast. The dough will not rise: the bread comes out small and heavy.
Yeast works faster at first, then dies at about 60 °C. The bread stops rising once it sets.
Gives flavour and controls the yeast. Too much, or salt touching the yeast, slows or damages it.
Feeds the yeast. A **lot** of sugar slows it down, because it draws water out of the yeast cells.

head: Type
How it is sold
How to use it
rows: Keep in the fridge; crumble into the dough or cream it with a little lukewarm water; use about double the weight of dried yeast.
Stir into lukewarm water with a pinch of sugar for about 10 minutes, until frothy.
Mix straight into the flour; no activation needed.

ul: Check the date on the packet. Old yeast is weak. Keep opened packets sealed in a cool place or the fridge.
Weigh yeast accurately: too much gives a yeasty taste and a collapsed loaf; too little gives a heavy loaf.

Use **strong (bread) flour** for most yeast doughs. Its high protein forms strong, stretchy **gluten** when mixed with water and kneaded. The gluten traps the gas and gives the bread its shape and chew.
Plain flour makes a softer, less stretchy dough: it is used for some buns and soft rolls.

head: Ingredient
Its job
rows: Makes the gluten, dissolves the salt and yeast; must be lukewarm. Milk makes a softer crumb and a browner crust.
Flavour; strengthens gluten; controls the yeast. About 2% of the flour weight is typical. **Do not put it directly on the yeast when you weigh them out.**
A little feeds the yeast and helps the crust brown. More makes a sweet dough.
Softens the crumb, keeps the bread fresh longer, and adds flavour.
Richness and colour in enriched doughs; egg wash for a shine.
For Jamaican buns and coco bread.

blocks.p: A **plain dough** has only flour, yeast, salt and water (and sometimes a little sugar or fat). An **enriched dough** has extra ingredients such as butter, milk, coconut milk, sugar, eggs, spices or dried fruit. Examples: **coco bread**, sweet buns, cinnamon rolls, brioche.

Fat and sugar slow the yeast, so enriched doughs often need more yeast or a longer proof. They brown faster in the oven, so they are often baked at a lower heat than plain bread, and covered if they brown too soon.

ul: Weigh **all** ingredients, including the water, because small changes alter the dough.
Bakers often give amounts as a percentage of the flour weight. Example: 1,500 g flour with 2% salt needs 2% x 1,500 = 30 g of salt.
Water is usually about 55–65% of the flour weight for rolls and loaves. A dough with too much water is sticky; too little makes a hard dough.
Keep the dough at about 25–27 °C after mixing. In Jamaica's heat, use cold water in summer, and chill the flour if the kitchen is very hot.

blocks.note: Water in Jamaican bakeries can come from the mains, a tank or a well, and tank water can be warm. Always test the water temperature on your wrist before it goes onto the yeast. If it feels hot, it is too hot.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Tool
Use
rows: Weigh in grams; measure water exactly.
Mixing bowls; mixer with dough hook
Cut, lift and scrape dough from the bench.
Cuts a large mass of dough into equal-weight pieces.
Roll flat doughs such as coco bread.
Gives gentle warmth and moisture for the final proof.
A flat wooden paddle for putting loaves into a deck oven and taking them out.
A convection oven has a fan that moves the hot air around.
Scores the top of a loaf.
Check the water and dough temperature.

sections.title: Mixing, kneading and the first proof

head: Method
How it works
Used for
rows: All the ingredients are mixed together at once.
Rolls, loaves, hard dough bread: the usual method
Part of the flour, water and all the yeast are mixed and left to ferment into a 'sponge'; the rest of the ingredients are added later.
Richer flavour; large batches; some enriched doughs

flow: Wash hands; put on a clean apron and cover the hair
Weigh the flour, salt, sugar, yeast, fat and water; keep the salt and yeast apart
Check the water: lukewarm, about 35–40 °C
Mix everything to a rough dough in the bowl or mixer
Knead until smooth, stretchy and elastic
Check with the stretch test
Shape the dough into a ball, put it in a lightly oiled bowl and cover it

blocks.p: **Kneading develops the gluten.** Flour proteins join with water and, when you work the dough, form long, stretchy strands. These trap the gas from the yeast, so the dough rises and holds its shape. Kneading also spreads the yeast evenly through the dough.

ul: By hand: put the dough on a clean, lightly floured bench. Push it away from you with the heel of your hand, fold it back over, turn it a quarter, and push again. Keep a steady rhythm for about 8–10 minutes, or as the recipe says.
With a mixer: use the dough hook on a low to medium speed for about 6–10 minutes. Stay with the machine.
At first the dough is rough and sticky. Do not add lots of extra flour, or the bread will be dry and heavy. Knead on and it becomes smooth and soft.

blocks.p: Take a small piece of dough and stretch it gently between your fingers. When it is ready, it stretches into a **thin, see-through sheet without tearing**. If it tears at once, knead for longer.

ul: Put the dough in a lightly oiled bowl and **cover it** with cling film or a damp cloth, so that a skin does not form.
Leave it in a **warm place free from draughts** until it has about **doubled in size**. This usually takes about an hour in a warm room, longer in a cool one.
During the first proof the yeast makes gas, the dough rises and the flavour develops.
A dough left too long becomes sour, weak and sticky.

blocks.note: A warm Jamaican kitchen makes dough prove faster than the recipe time. Check the dough by looking at it, not the clock alone.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Knocking back, scaling, shaping and final proof

blocks.p: **Knocking back** means pressing out the gas from the risen dough with your fist, then gently kneading for a short time. It evens out the gas bubbles, redistributes the yeast and food, and prepares the dough for shaping. Do not tear the dough.
**Scaling** means weighing the dough into equal pieces. Use the scales: do not guess. Equal pieces bake evenly, look neat, give fair portions and make costing accurate.

ul: Example: 2.4 kg of dough scaled into 60 g rolls gives 2,400 / 60 = **40 rolls**.
Allow a little for loss and trimming. Check three pieces on the scales after you have scaled the rest.
Keep scaled pieces covered while you work so that the surface does not dry.

blocks.p: After scaling, roll each piece into a **tight round ball** by cupping your hand over it on the bench and rolling in a circle. This gives a smooth skin that holds the gas and a neat, even shape. Rest the rounds for a few minutes, then shape.

head: Shape
How to make it
rows: Roll the piece into a tight ball with a smooth top.
Roll the ball into a short sausage with tapered ends.
Roll a rope about 15 cm long and tie a single knot; tuck in the ends.
Roll three ropes, join them at one end, plait and tuck the ends under.
Flatten the dough, roll it up tightly like a Swiss roll, seal the seam and place seam-side down in a greased tin.
Roll a round piece flat, brush with butter and fold in half.

ul: Place shaped pieces on lined or greased trays with space between them, or in greased tins.
Keep the seam underneath so that it does not split open.
Cover the shaped dough and leave it in a **warm, moist place**, often a prover set as the maker says, so that it rises again before baking.
Gentle warmth and moisture keep the surface soft, so that the dough can expand.

**Finger test:** press a floured finger gently into the dough. If the dent **springs back slowly** and partly, the dough is ready. If it springs back fast, it needs longer. If the dent stays and the dough sighs, it is **over-proved**.
Bake at once. Dough that waits too long collapses.

head: Stage
Typical conditions
Sign that it is ready
rows: Covered, warm and moist (about 30–35 °C), about 30–60 minutes

blocks.note: Times and temperatures change with the dough, the yeast and the room. Use the signs (doubled size; slow spring-back), not only the timing.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: **Egg wash** (beaten egg, often with a little milk or water) brushed on just before baking gives a shine and a golden colour. List egg as an allergen.
Seeds such as sesame can be sprinkled on the wet egg wash. Label sesame.
**Scoring** means cutting the top of a loaf with a sharp blade before baking. It controls where the loaf opens up in the oven, so that it does not burst in a random place.

**Preheat** the oven. Plain rolls and loaves bake in a hot oven, about **200–230 °C**, as the recipe and oven maker say. Enriched doughs (coco bread, buns) are often baked at a lower heat, about 180–200 °C, because the sugar, milk and fat make them brown faster.
In the first minutes the dough rises quickly. This is **oven spring**: the heat makes the gas expand and the yeast works fast before it dies. Do not open the door in this time.
Bake rolls for about 12–20 minutes and loaves for about 30–40 minutes, or as the recipe says. Turn the tray if the oven bakes unevenly.
Use dry oven gloves and a peel.

blocks.h: How to tell that bread is baked

ul: The crust is an even golden brown.
Take the loaf out of the tin and **tap the base**: it sounds **hollow**. A dull sound means the middle is not yet baked.
Rolls are light for their size and golden all round.
Cool bread on a **wire rack**, so that steam can escape from all sides and the base stays dry. On a solid surface it sweats and the crust goes soft.
Do not wrap or slice bread until it is completely cool. Warm bread wrapped in a bag sweats and goes mouldy. Cutting warm bread squashes the crumb.
Brush coco bread and buns with melted butter or sugar syrup after baking for a soft top or a shiny glaze.

head: Fault
Likely cause
How to prevent it
rows: Small, heavy bread with a tight crumb
Yeast killed by hot liquid; too little yeast; under-proved; too much salt; too little kneading
Check the water temperature; weigh the yeast; prove until doubled; knead properly
Collapsed, large holes, sour or yeasty taste
Watch the dough; use the finger test; bake as soon as it is ready
Oven too cool; baked too briefly; too little sugar
Preheat; bake until golden and hollow-sounding
Oven too hot; too much sugar or milk
Lower the heat; cover with foil if it browns too soon
Hard skin and dry patches on the dough
Too much flour added while kneading; too little water
Weigh the ingredients; do not add extra flour
Under-proved; no scoring; oven too hot at first
Stored in the fridge; not enough fat; stored warm
Keep at room temperature, or freeze

blocks.note: If the dough is sticky, do not add lots of flour. Knead a little longer: gluten development makes it less sticky. If it stays very sticky, check the amount of water weighed.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Jamaican **hard dough bread** is a dense, close-textured, slightly sweet loaf with a soft crust, traditionally baked in a tin. It is the daily bread of many homes, eaten with butter, cheese or fried eggs and with ackee and saltfish.

flow: Weigh strong flour, sugar, salt, yeast and shortening or butter; keep the salt and yeast apart
Mix with lukewarm water to a firm dough
Knead until smooth and firm
Prove, covered, until doubled
Knock back, scale and shape into a tight loaf
Place seam-side down in a greased tin and give a final proof
Bake at the heat the recipe and oven maker say until golden and hollow-sounding when tapped underneath
Cool on a rack; slice only when cool

ul: The dough is firmer and stiffer than a roll dough, which gives the close crumb.
Turn the loaf out on a board away from your body, to avoid steam burns.

blocks.p: **Coco bread** is a soft, slightly sweet, enriched roll made with coconut milk and butter, folded in half so that it can be opened and filled with a patty. It is made by the straight dough method.

flow: Weigh strong flour, sugar, salt and yeast; keep the salt and yeast apart
Warm coconut milk to lukewarm; melt the butter
Mix to a soft dough and knead until smooth and stretchy
Prove, covered, until doubled
Knock back and scale into equal pieces; round each one
Roll each piece into a flat oval or round and brush with butter
Fold in half and place on a lined tray; give the final proof
Bake until lightly golden, then brush with butter so that it stays soft
Label the allergens: wheat and milk

blocks.h: Spiced buns and other sweet goods

blocks.p: A Jamaican spiced bun is dark, sticky and rich with molasses, spices and dried fruit, and is often eaten with cheese at Easter. Some bakeries make it with yeast and others with baking powder, so follow the Centre's recipe. A **sugar syrup glaze** is brushed on straight after baking so that the top is shiny and sticky. Also in this group are cinnamon rolls, sweet buns and brioche.

flow: Make an enriched dough, prove it, knock back, scale and shape rings or rounds
Give the final proof on lightly floured trays or squares of paper
Heat the oil to about 170–190 °C, or as the recipe and fryer maker say, checking with a thermometer
Lift the doughnuts carefully and lower them **gently away from you** into the oil
Fry for about 1–2 minutes a side; turn once with a slotted spoon when the first side is golden
Lift out and drain on kitchen paper
Toss in sugar, or fill and ice when cool

head: Frying rule
Why
rows: Fill the fryer only to the line, never above it
Oil can overflow and catch fire.
Keep the area dry; no water near hot oil
Water makes hot oil spit violently.
The oil cools and the doughnuts become greasy.
Lower doughnuts gently, away from you
Stops hot oil from splashing onto you.
Keep a fire blanket and the correct extinguisher close by
You must be ready before anything goes wrong.
If oil catches fire: turn off the heat and cover with a fire blanket
Never use water. Do not move the pan. Call for help.
Too cool: doughnuts are greasy. Too hot: they burn outside and stay raw inside
Use the thermostat or a thermometer.

blocks.note: Never put water on a fat or oil fire. It spreads the fire. Turn off the heat, smother the fire with a fire blanket or a lid, and call for help.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Product
What it is
rows: A long, thin French loaf with a crisp crust.
An Italian flat bread topped with olive oil, salt and herbs.
A flat, round bread with a pocket inside.
Yeast doughs **layered with butter** (laminated), like puff pastry, so that they are flaky.
A very rich dough with eggs and butter.

blocks.h: Plan back from the time of service

blocks.p: Yeast goods must be fresh and ready on time. Work **backwards** from the time they are needed, adding up each stage.

ul: Example: rolls needed at 7:00 a.m. Add up cooling 30, baking 20, final proof 45, shaping 20, first proof 60 and mixing 30: 205 minutes (3 hours 25 minutes). Start at about 3:30 a.m., allowing a few spare minutes.
Check that ingredients are in stock and the mixer, prover and oven are free and working. Switch the oven on early enough to be hot.
Dough can be slowed in the fridge overnight so that it is ready to shape and bake early in the morning.
Write the plan on a production sheet and check the dough at each stage. In warm weather, dough proves faster.

head: Product
How to store it
rows: Covered or in a clean bread bin, cool and dry, away from pests.
Yeast goods with cream or custard
Covered in the fridge at 5 °C or below, or as the Centre's food safety plan says.
Covered, oiled and chilled in the fridge.

ul: **Do not keep bread in the fridge.** At about 5 °C bread goes stale fastest. The freezer stops staling.
Do not wrap bread while it is warm.
Label every product with its **name, date made and allergens**, and use stock first in, first out.
Make rolls the **same size and shape** so that they look neat, portions are fair and costs are accurate.
Serve warm rolls in a clean basket lined with a napkin, using tongs or gloves.
Label seeded breads for sesame and other allergens.
Keep a few spare so that the basket can be refilled.
Use stale bread for bread and butter pudding or breadcrumbs, as the kitchen's plan allows.
Wash, rinse, sanitise and dry the bowl, hook, scrapers and trays. Switch off and unplug machines.
Wipe the bench and sweep the floor. Report faulty equipment, low stock and accidents.
I can list the rules of personal hygiene and name the allergens in yeast goods.
I can use the mixer, the oven and a deep fryer safely, and deal with an oil fire.
I can say what yeast is and what it needs, and explain the effect of heat, salt and sugar.
I can name the types of yeast and the job of each ingredient.
I can weigh accurately and use baker's percentages.
I can make a straight dough, and say what the sponge-and-dough method is.
I can explain why we knead and use the stretch test.
I can carry out the first proof, knock back, scale, round and shape.
I can make round rolls, knots, plaits and a tin loaf.
I can use the finger test for the final proof.
I can bake, test with a tap on the base, and cool bread correctly.
I can name common faults in bread, their causes and their cures.
I can make hard dough bread, coco bread and yeast doughnuts.
I can plan the baking backwards from the time of service.
I can store, freeze, label and present yeast goods, and clean down.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step, not only the step. For example: 'I cover the dough while it proves so that the surface does not dry and form a skin.'
blocks.label: Tip

Yeast turning sugar into gas and alcohol.
The stretchy network formed by flour proteins and water, which traps gas.
Bread flour with a high protein content.

Stretching a small piece of dough thin without tearing, to check the gluten.
A method in which all the ingredients are mixed at once.
A method in which part of the flour, water and yeast is fermented first.
The first rise of the whole dough, covered, in a warm place.
Pressing out the gas after the first proof.
Rolling a piece into a tight ball.
The second rise, of the shaped dough, before baking.
A cabinet that gives warmth and moisture for proving.
Left to rise too long, so that it collapses and tastes sour.
The quick rise of dough in the first minutes of baking.
Cutting the top of a loaf to control how it opens.
Beaten egg brushed on for a shine.
The soft inside of a loaf.
A dough with added butter, milk, sugar, egg, spices or fruit.
Dough layered with butter, as in croissants.
A flat paddle for putting bread into an oven.
A dense, slightly sweet Jamaican loaf.
A soft Jamaican roll made with coconut milk, folded in half.
Bread becoming hard and dry, fastest in the fridge.

c1.title: Rolls for a breakfast buffet in Ocho Rios
c1.text: Chef Marcia plans to have 40 bread rolls ready at 7:00 a.m. for a hotel breakfast in Ocho Rios. Trainee Dwight mixes his dough at 4:30 a.m., using water straight from a tank that has been warmed by the sun; it feels hot to his wrist. He ignores the recipe's final proof, because he is behind. His rolls come out small, heavy and pale, with a tight crumb. Marcia asks him to work out the time and fix the plan for next time.

c2.title: Hard dough bread in a May Pen bakery
c2.text: At a bakery in May Pen, trainee Shelly makes hard dough bread. After eight minutes of kneading, a small piece of her dough tears as soon as she stretches it. She puts it in a bowl, uncovered, in a warm spot. When she tries the bread after baking, the crust has a hard skin and the loaf has dense dry patches. She cuts a loaf while it is still hot and the crumb squashes. She wraps the rest in a bag while still warm.

c3.title: Doughnuts at a café in Negril
c3.text: A beach café in Negril sells yeast doughnuts. Trainee Andre fills the fryer to the brim with oil and, in a hurry, drops in twelve doughnuts together from a height. The oil splashes and the doughnuts come out greasy and pale. When he turns around to take a call, the oil starts to smoke and catches fire.

c4.title: Coco bread for an order in Falmouth
c4.text: A Falmouth bakery gets an order for 60 coco breads for a church function, to be filled with patties. The dough is made with lukewarm coconut milk and melted butter, and the whole batch of dough weighs 4.5 kg. Trainee Latoya scales the dough into 75 g pieces. The baker tells her the salt must not be put on the yeast when the ingredients are weighed out. After baking she brushes the coco breads with butter and prints labels.

c5.title: Storing bread at a Montego Bay hotel
c5.text: A hotel kitchen in Montego Bay bakes dinner rolls on Monday, sprinkled with sesame seeds. The chef puts the leftovers in the fridge, and by Tuesday they are hard. The kitchen also needs to keep 30 rolls for Thursday. A trainee has a small cut on a finger while shaping the next batch of rolls.

questions.q: Why did Dwight's rolls come out small and heavy?
o: The yeast was weakened by water that was too hot
The dough was proved for far too long before baking
He used strong flour in the dough instead of plain flour
The oven was far too hot when the rolls went into it
questions.why: Water above about 55 °C kills yeast, so little gas forms and the bread stays small and heavy. Test the water on your wrist: it should feel only warm.

questions.q: How should Dwight have tested the water?
o: By checking that steam rises from it before he mixes
By touching it with his wrist, so it feels lukewarm
By checking that it is cold enough to look quite clear
By dipping a finger in to see whether it is warm enough
questions.why: Lukewarm water, about 35–40 °C, feels only comfortably warm on the wrist. If it feels hot, it will damage the yeast. Use a thermometer when you can.

questions.q: Marcia's plan: cooling 30 min, baking 20, final proof 45, shaping 20, first proof 60, mixing 30. When should work start for a 7:00 a.m. service, ignoring spare time?
questions.why: The stages add up to 30 + 20 + 45 + 20 + 60 + 30 = 205 minutes, which is 3 hours 25 minutes. Counting back from 7:00 a.m. gives 3:35 a.m.; allow a few spare minutes.

questions.q: What does skipping the final proof do to the rolls?
o: It makes the crust thicker and a darker brown
It leaves too little gas, so the rolls stay small and dense
It makes the rolls rise too much and then collapse in the oven
It has no effect at all, as the oven does all of the rising
questions.why: The final proof lets the shaped dough rise again before baking. Without it the rolls are dense. Test with the finger press: the dent should spring back slowly.

questions.q: Shelly's dough tears at once when stretched. What does that show?
o: It has been over-proved and must be baked at once
The gluten is not yet developed, so she should knead longer
The flour was too weak, so she should add a lot more yeast
It has too much water, so she should add more flour to it
questions.why: Dough that tears quickly has not formed strong gluten. Knead on until a small piece stretches into a thin, see-through sheet without tearing.

questions.q: Why did the crust of Shelly's loaf have a hard skin?
o: The oven was too cool when she put the loaf in to bake
She brushed too much egg wash over the top of the loaf
She left the dough uncovered while it proved and it dried
She kneaded the dough for too long a time before proving it
questions.why: Uncovered dough dries on the surface and forms a skin that does not stretch, leaving hard patches. Always cover the dough while it proves.

questions.q: How can Shelly check that her loaf is fully baked?
o: Tap the base of the loaf and listen for a hollow sound
Press the top crust and see whether it feels quite soft
Look at the colour of the top crust and nothing else
Cut the loaf in half while it is still hot from the oven
questions.why: A baked loaf sounds hollow when tapped underneath. A dull sound means the middle is still doughy. Cutting a hot loaf squashes the crumb.

questions.q: What should Shelly do with the rest of the bread?
o: Wrap it while warm, so that it keeps its heat in the bag
Put it in the fridge so that it cools down faster
Cover it with a damp cloth and leave it on the bench
Cool it on a wire rack and wrap it when completely cold
questions.why: Steam must escape or the bread sweats and may grow mould. A wire rack lets air circulate round the loaf; wrap it only when cold.

questions.q: Why did Andre's doughnuts come out greasy and pale?
o: The oil was too hot, so the dough burned
The dough had too little yeast, so it did not rise
The oil cooled when he added too many at once
He used too much sugar in the dough, which made it soft
questions.why: A crowded fryer drops the oil temperature, so the doughnuts soak up oil instead of crisping. Fry in small batches at about 170–190 °C, or as the recipe says.

questions.q: What is the safest way to put doughnuts into hot oil?
o: Drop them from a height so that they sink quickly
Lower them gently, away from you
Throw them in quickly and step back at once
Lower them gently, leaning close to watch
questions.why: Lowering them gently, away from your body, stops hot oil splashing onto your hands and face.

questions.q: The oil is on fire. What should Andre do first?
o: Carry the pan outside to let the oil cool down
Pour water over the flames to put them out quickly
Turn off the heat and cover the pan with a fire blanket
Throw a handful of flour over the flames to smother them
questions.why: Water makes burning oil spread violently. Turn off the heat, cover the pan with a fire blanket or lid, do not move it, and call for help.

questions.q: The dough weighs 4.5 kg and Latoya scales 75 g pieces. How many coco breads is that?
questions.why: 4,500 g divided by 75 g is 60, which matches the order. Allow for a little loss and check three pieces on the scales.

questions.q: Why is the salt kept away from the yeast when weighing?
o: It makes the yeast taste of salt in the bread
Direct contact with salt can slow or damage the yeast
The salt would dissolve before the dough is even made
It stops the salt from spreading evenly through the dough
questions.why: Salt draws water out of yeast cells and slows or damages them. Weigh them in separate piles and mix the salt in with the flour.

questions.q: Why is coconut milk warmed only to lukewarm for the dough?
o: Hot coconut milk would kill the yeast
Hot coconut milk would turn the dough yellow
Cold coconut milk would make the dough too sweet
Hot coconut milk would change the flavour of the bread
questions.why: Yeast dies in liquid above about 55 °C. Lukewarm liquid wakes it up without harming it.

questions.q: Which allergens must be on the label of the coco breads?
o: Wheat and milk
Wheat and sesame
Eggs and sesame
Milk and nuts
questions.why: Coco bread is made from wheat flour and butter, so the label shows wheat (gluten) and milk. Add egg if egg wash is used, and sesame if seeds are put on top.

questions.q: Why were the leftover rolls hard by Tuesday?
o: The fridge makes bread go stale faster
The sesame seeds took the moisture from the rolls
The rolls were wrapped while they were warm
The rolls were baked at too low a heat
questions.why: At about 5 °C bread stales fastest. Keep bread at room temperature for a day, and freeze it for longer.

questions.q: How should the 30 rolls for Thursday be kept?
o: On the bench in a covered basket until Thursday morning
In the fridge, wrapped, until they are needed
Wrapped, labelled and frozen, then thawed on the day
In the oven on a very low heat so that they stay fresh
questions.why: Freezing stops staling. Wrap the rolls, label them with the date, and thaw them on the day, refreshing in the oven if needed.

questions.q: What must the trainee do about the cut on his finger before shaping rolls?
o: Cover it with a blue plaster and a glove, and report it
Wipe it with a cloth and carry on shaping the rolls
Wash it and carry on, because the dough will be baked
Cover it with a plain bandage from the first aid box
questions.why: A cut must be cleaned and covered with a waterproof, brightly coloured plaster and a glove, so that it cannot touch the food and a lost plaster can be seen.

questions.q: A recipe uses 750 g of flour and salt at 2% of the flour weight. How much salt is needed?
questions.why: 2% of 750 g is 0.02 x 750 = 15 g. Remember to keep the salt away from the yeast when weighing.

questions.q: A hotel needs fresh rolls at 6:30 a.m., but the baker finishes shaping the dough at 9 p.m. the evening before. What is the best way to keep the shaped dough until morning?
o: Cover it and chill it, then give it a final proof and bake it in the morning
Leave it uncovered on the bench, so that it can dry out a little overnight
Put it in the oven with the heat off, so that it stays warm and keeps rising
Freeze it and put it straight into a hot oven without thawing
questions.why: The cold slows the yeast right down, so the dough keeps overnight without over-proving. Cover it so that it does not dry, then bring it to room temperature for the final proof and bake it in the morning.
